plotSections.title: Gerk and the Mother's Prayer
bullets: The prophecy heard repeatedly in the stronghold is identified as the Mother's Prayer, also called the Mother's Tale. Gerk is confirmed as the child described by the prophecy and the potential keeper who will open the doors.

Plymouth questions Gerk about whether he believes he is the foretold individual. Gerk remains uncertain and says he is simply doing what makes him happy: smashing things and traveling with his friends.

Plymouth explains that the prophecy is not merely a generic description. It contains factual information connected to Gerk's life and the people close to him, strengthening the case that Gerk is the foretold child.

The Mother's Prayer is a sacred prophecy of the Navi whose origin is unknown. It has been recorded in multiple journals by different authors, generally following a pattern of catastrophe, a hero's story, and eventually difficult choices that the hero must make.

The prophecy does not dictate Gerk's actions or explain exactly how he arrived at his current circumstances. His choices remain his own, and the recorded Mother's Tales can apparently change or rewrite themselves if a son or daughter of the tree chooses to follow a different path.

The prophecy is described through a tree-and-fruit metaphor: the Mother's Prayer is the tree, while its chosen heroes are the fruit produced by it. The tree has dwindled and is now in grave circumstances.

Plymouth reveals that Gerk is one of the sons and daughters of the Great Tree and that he is the first such individual in roughly 1,500 years to come forward and potentially accept the role described by the Mother's Prayer.
Plymouth has previously communicated with three other sons or daughters of the Great Tree. One accepted the challenge, while the other two apparently did not continue with it.

Gerk is offered a choice: he can effectively 'fall from the tree' and reject the role, or allow himself to be 'plucked from it' and accept guidance toward fulfilling the role. Gerk agrees to proceed if doing so will help Atlas.

Plymouth then explains that Gerk's decision affects not only Gerk but potentially all of Atlas. The rest of the party is now involved because there are stipulations concerning the camaraderie between the chosen child and his friends.
The choice remains voluntary for the other party members, although refusing to participate could potentially affect their relationship with Gerk. Gerk's choice takes precedence in this matter.

chronologicalEvents: Dana recites the prophecy heard echoing through the stronghold, describing gates opening, eight being torn asunder, sleeping keys, and arches as doors waiting to awaken.
The prophecy is identified as the Mother's Prayer or Mother's Tale, and Gerk is identified as its subject and the child who will open the doors.
Plymouth approaches Gerk and asks whether he believes he is the individual described by the Mother's Prayer.
Gerk says he does not know whether he is the chosen person and explains that he is simply doing what makes him happy.
Plymouth challenges Gerk to consider whether he is strong enough to accept whatever responsibility might be bestowed upon him.
Plymouth reveals that the Mother's Prayer is an ancient sacred prophecy of the Navi, with an unknown original seer and many versions recorded by different authors.
Plymouth explains that the prophecy traditionally involves a catastrophe, a hero, and increasingly difficult choices for that hero.
Plymouth confirms that Gerk is the person spoken of by the prophecy and one of the sons or daughters of the Great Tree.
Plymouth explains that the prophecy does not remove Gerk's agency; his past choices were still his own, and the prophecy did not determine how he reached this point.
Plymouth says Mother's Tales can rewrite themselves when a son or daughter of the tree chooses to follow their own path.
Plymouth reveals that he has communicated with three other sons or daughters of the Great Tree, but none has taken up the role for approximately 1,500 years.
Gerk asks how they can know the prophecy truly refers to him rather than one of many possible people.
Plymouth points to specific factual information in the prophecy concerning someone close to Gerk as evidence that it is more specific than a generic description.
Gerk agrees to accept the path if doing so can help Atlas.
Plymouth explains that Gerk's acceptance brings the rest of the party into the situation because the chosen child's relationship with his companions has associated stipulations.

notes: Confirmed to be the child foretold by the Mother's Prayer/Mother's Tale.
Confirmed to be one of the sons or daughters of the Great Tree.
Gerk initially remains skeptical that he is the chosen individual and says he is simply doing what makes him happy by smashing things and traveling with his friends.
Gerk accepts the path associated with the prophecy when told that doing so could help all of Atlas.
His personal choices remain his own; the prophecy describes him but does not dictate how he reached his current position or what choices he must make.
Gerk's choice to accept the role brings the rest of the party into the situation because of stated stipulations concerning the chosen child and his friends.
